claim: Mps1 is the master spindle checkpoint kinase that senses kinetochore-microtubule attachment and promotes checkpoint signaling to ensure accurate chromosome segregation.
source: The master spindle checkpoint kinase Mps1 senses kinetochore-microtubule attachment and promotes checkpoint signaling to ensure accurate chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of Mps1, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Knl1, when phosphorylated by Mps1, recruits checkpoint complexes Bub1–Bub3 and BubR1–Bub3 to unattached kinetochores.
source: The kinetochore scaffold Knl1, when phosphorylated by Mps1, recruits checkpoint complexes Bub1–Bub3 and BubR1–Bub3 to unattached kinetochores.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and represents established knowledge about the checkpoint mechanism.

claim: Active checkpoint signaling enhances the assembly of the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC) consisting of BubR1–Bub3, Mad2, and Cdc20.
source: Active checkpoint signaling ultimately enhances the assembly of the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC) consisting of BubR1–Bub3, Mad2, and Cdc20, which inhibits the anaphase-promoting complex or cyclosome bound to Cdc20 (APC/CCdc20) to delay anaphase onset.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about checkpoint signaling.

claim: MCC inhibits APC/CCdc20 to delay anaphase onset.
source: Active checkpoint signaling ultimately enhances the assembly of the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC) consisting of BubR1–Bub3, Mad2, and Cdc20, which inhibits the anaphase-promoting complex or cyclosome bound to Cdc20 (APC/CCdc20) to delay anaphase onset.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about MCC function.

claim: Mps1 promotes APC/C inhibition by MCC components through phosphorylating Bub1 and Mad1.
source: Using in vitro reconstitution, we show that Mps1 promotes APC/C inhibition by MCC components through phosphorylating Bub1 and Mad1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: Phosphorylated Bub1 binds to Mad1–Mad2.
source: Phosphorylated Bub1 binds to Mad1–Mad2.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through binding assays in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylated Mad1 directly interacts with Cdc20.
source: Phosphorylated Mad1 directly interacts with Cdc20.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through binding assays in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations of Mps1 phosphorylation sites in Bub1 or Mad1 abrogate the spindle checkpoint in human cells.
source: Mutations of Mps1 phosphorylation sites in Bub1 or Mad1 abrogate the spindle checkpoint in human cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through cellular experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Mps1 promotes checkpoint activation through sequentially phosphorylating Knl1, Bub1, and Mad1.
source: Therefore, Mps1 promotes checkpoint activation through sequentially phosphorylating Knl1, Bub1, and Mad1.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The sequential multi-target phosphorylation cascade makes the checkpoint highly responsive to Mps1 and to kinetochore-microtubule attachment.
source: This sequential multi-target phosphorylation cascade makes the checkpoint highly responsive to Mps1 and to kinetochore-microtubule attachment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about the phosphorylation cascade.

claim: The spindle checkpoint senses kinetochores that are not attached or improperly attached to spindle microtubules.
source: During mitosis, the spindle checkpoint senses kinetochores that are not attached or improperly attached to spindle microtubules and enhances the production of the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC) consisting of BubR1–Bub3, Mad2, and Cdc20 (Fang, 2002; Sudakin et al., 2001; Tang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MCC inhibits the ubiquitin ligase activity of APC/CCdc20.
source: MCC inhibits the ubiquitin ligase activity of the anaphase-promoting complex or cyclosome bound to its activator Cdc20 (APC/CCdc20) (Alfieri et al., 2016; Izawa and Pines, 2015; Yamaguchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Inhibition of APC/CCdc20 delays anaphase onset until all kinetochores achieve proper kinetochore-microtubule attachment.
source: Inhibition of APC/CCdc20 delays anaphase onset until all kinetochores in a mitotic cell achieve proper kinetochore-microtubule attachment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the checkpoint mechanism.

claim: A dysfunctional spindle checkpoint causes chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy.
source: A dysfunctional spindle checkpoint causes chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, which have been implicated in cancers, birth defects, and other human diseases (Gorbsky, 2015; Holland and Cleveland, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy have been implicated in cancers, birth defects, and other human diseases.
source: A dysfunctional spindle checkpoint causes chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, which have been implicated in cancers, birth defects, and other human diseases (Gorbsky, 2015; Holland and Cleveland, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mps1 recognizes unattached kinetochores through binding to the Ndc80 complex when it is not bound by microtubules.
source: Mps1 recognizes unattached kinetochores through binding to the critical microtubule receptor, the Ndc80 complex (Ndc80C), when it is not bound by microtubules (Hiruma et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ndc80C-bound Mps1 initiates checkpoint signaling by phosphorylating multiple MELT motifs of Knl1.
source: Ndc80C-bound Mps1 initiates checkpoint signaling by phosphorylating multiple methionine-glutamate-leucine-threonine (MELT) motifs of the kinetochore scaffold Knl1 (London et al., 2012; Shepperd et al., 2012; Yamagishi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylated MELT motifs recruit checkpoint complexes Bub1–Bub3 and BubR1–Bub3 to the kinetochores.
source: Phosphorylated MELT motifs recruit checkpoint complexes Bub1–Bub3 and BubR1–Bub3 to the kinetochores (Krenn et al., 2014; Overlack et al., 2015; Primorac et al., 2013; Vleugel et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Bub1 and BubR1 recruit and modify Cdc20.
source: Bub1 and BubR1 in turn recruit and modify Cdc20 (Di Fiore et al., 2015; Diaz-Martinez et al., 2015; Han et al., 2014; Jia et al., 2016; Lischetti et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mad1–Mad2 is targeted to kinetochores through multiple mechanisms.
source: Mad1–Mad2 is also targeted to kinetochores through multiple mechanisms (Caldas et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2012; London and Biggins, 2014; Matson and Stukenberg, 2014; Silió et al., 2015), and promotes the conformational activation of open Mad2 (O-Mad2) to intermediate Mad2 (I-Mad2) (De Antoni et al., 2005; Hara et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2002, 2004; Luo and Yu, 2008; Mapelli et al., 2007; Mapelli and Musacchio, 2007; Sironi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mad1–Mad2 promotes the conformational activation of O-Mad2 to I-Mad2.
source: Mad1–Mad2 is also targeted to kinetochores through multiple mechanisms (Caldas et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2012; London and Biggins, 2014; Matson and Stukenberg, 2014; Silió et al., 2015), and promotes the conformational activation of open Mad2 (O-Mad2) to intermediate Mad2 (I-Mad2) (De Antoni et al., 2005; Hara et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2002, 2004; Luo and Yu, 2008; Mapelli et al., 2007; Mapelli and Musacchio, 2007; Sironi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: I-Mad2 is passed on to Cdc20 to form the Cdc20–C-Mad2 complex.
source: I-Mad2 is passed on to Cdc20 to form the Cdc20–C-Mad2 complex, which subsequently associates with BubR1–Bub3 to form MCC (Kulukian et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Cdc20–C-Mad2 complex associates with BubR1–Bub3 to form MCC.
source: I-Mad2 is passed on to Cdc20 to form the Cdc20–C-Mad2 complex, which subsequently associates with BubR1–Bub3 to form MCC (Kulukian et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: MCC diffuses from kinetochores to inhibit APC/CCdc20 throughout the cell.
source: MCC diffuses from kinetochores to inhibit APC/CCdc20 throughout the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MCC function.

claim: Artificial tethering of Mad1–Mad2 to attached kinetochores causes prolonged activation of the spindle checkpoint and delays anaphase onset in the absence of spindle poisons.
source: Artificial tethering of Mad1–Mad2 to attached kinetochores causes prolonged activation of the spindle checkpoint and delays anaphase onset in the absence of spindle poisons (Maldonado and Kapoor, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Artificial activation of the checkpoint by Mad1–Mad2 tethering still requires the kinase activity of Mps1.
source: This artificial activation of the checkpoint still requires the kinase activity of Mps1, indicating that, aside from Knl1 phosphorylation, Mps1 has downstream functions in the checkpoint.
evidence: This is established knowledge that supports the existence of additional Mps1 functions beyond Knl1 phosphorylation.

claim: Mps1 has downstream functions in the checkpoint aside from Knl1 phosphorylation.
source: This artificial activation of the checkpoint still requires the kinase activity of Mps1, indicating that, aside from Knl1 phosphorylation, Mps1 has downstream functions in the checkpoint.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Mad1–Mad2 tethering requires Mps1 activity.

claim: In budding and fission yeast, Mps1 phosphorylates Bub1 to establish a phosphorylation-dependent interaction between Bub1 and Mad1.
source: Studies in the budding and fission yeast suggest that one such function of Mps1 is to phosphorylate Bub1 and establish a phosphorylation-dependent interaction between Bub1 and Mad1 (London and Biggins, 2014; Mora-Santos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from yeast studies supported by citations.

claim: The RLK motif in the Mad1 C-terminal domain responsible for phospho-Bub1 binding is conserved from yeast to man.
source: Although the RLK motif in the Mad1 C-terminal domain (CTD) responsible for phospho-Bub1 binding is conserved from yeast to man (Brady and Hardwick, 2000; Kim et al., 2012), this Mps1-stimulated Bub1–Mad1 interaction has not been formally demonstrated in humans.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The Mps1-stimulated Bub1–Mad1 interaction has not been formally demonstrated in humans prior to this study.
source: Although the RLK motif in the Mad1 C-terminal domain (CTD) responsible for phospho-Bub1 binding is conserved from yeast to man (Brady and Hardwick, 2000; Kim et al., 2012), this Mps1-stimulated Bub1–Mad1 interaction has not been formally demonstrated in humans.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: There is a direct phosphorylation-dependent interaction between human Bub1 and Mad1 in vitro.
source: Here, we report a direct phosphorylation-dependent interaction between human Bub1 and Mad1 in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through in vitro binding assays.

claim: The Bub1–Mad1 interaction requires phosphorylation of Bub1 by both Cdk1 and Mps1.
source: This interaction requires phosphorylation of Bub1 by both Cdk1 and Mps1, and is critical for spindle checkpoint activation in human cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through in vitro kinase and binding assays.

claim: The Bub1–Mad1 interaction is critical for spindle checkpoint activation in human cells.
source: This interaction requires phosphorylation of Bub1 by both Cdk1 and Mps1, and is critical for spindle checkpoint activation in human cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through cellular experiments.

claim: Checkpoint-dependent APC/CCdc20 inhibition by MCC components has been reconstituted in vitro.
source: We have in vitro reconstituted checkpoint-dependent APC/CCdc20 inhibition by MCC components, which requires a functional phospho-Bub1–Mad1 scaffold.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: Checkpoint-dependent APC/CCdc20 inhibition requires a functional phospho-Bub1–Mad1 scaffold.
source: We have in vitro reconstituted checkpoint-dependent APC/CCdc20 inhibition by MCC components, which requires a functional phospho-Bub1–Mad1 scaffold.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: Mps1 directly phosphorylates Mad1 in its C-terminal domain.
source: Furthermore, we have found that Mps1 directly phosphorylates Mad1 in its CTD.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through in vitro kinase assays and mass spectrometry.

claim: Phosphorylated Mad1 CTD directly binds to the N-terminal region of Cdc20.
source: Phosphorylated Mad1 CTD directly binds to the N-terminal region of Cdc20 and contributes to APC/CCdc20 inhibition presumably through stimulating MCC assembly.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through binding assays.

claim: Phosphorylated Mad1 CTD contributes to APC/CCdc20 inhibition presumably through stimulating MCC assembly.
source: Phosphorylated Mad1 CTD directly binds to the N-terminal region of Cdc20 and contributes to APC/CCdc20 inhibition presumably through stimulating MCC assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data, with the mechanism being inferred.

claim: Phosphorylation of Knl1 by Mps1 enables Bub1 recruitment.
source: Phosphorylation of Knl1 by Mps1 enables Bub1 recruitment.
evidence: This is part of the sequential phosphorylation cascade described in the study.

claim: Phosphorylation of Bub1 by Mps1 establishes the Bub1–Mad1 interaction.
source: Phosphorylation of Bub1 by Mps1 establishes the Bub1–Mad1 interaction.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through in vitro experiments.

claim: Phosphorylation of Mad1 by Mps1 positions Cdc20 for MCC assembly.
source: Phosphorylation of Mad1 by Mps1 positions Cdc20 for MCC assembly.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through in vitro experiments.

claim: The sequential multi-target phosphorylation cascade keeps the final signaling output responsive to kinetochore attachment status.
source: We propose that this sequential multi-target phosphorylation cascade makes the checkpoint highly responsive to Mps1 whose function is directly regulated by kinetochore-microtubule attachment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about the phosphorylation cascade.

claim: Bub1 is highly phosphorylated in mitosis.
source: Bub1 is highly phosphorylated in mitosis (Chen, 2004; Tang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 30 phosphorylated residues were identified in the non-kinase domain of Bub1 from mitotic HeLa cells.
source: We identified 30 phosphorylated residues that were scattered in the non-kinase domain of Bub1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from mass spectrometry analysis of endogenous Bub1.

claim: Bub1 S459 is located in the Bub1 conserved middle region (CM).
source: One such site, S459, is located in the Bub1 CM.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the mass spectrometry data and sequence analysis.

claim: Recombinant Bub1ΔK–Bub3 is strongly phosphorylated at S459 by recombinant Cdk1, but not Mps1, in vitro.
source: Recombinant Bub1ΔK–Bub3 was strongly phosphorylated at S459 by recombinant Cdk1, but not Mps1, in vitro (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Bub1 S459 is followed by a proline and matches the minimal Cdk1 substrate consensus of [S/T]P.
source: This finding is consistent with the fact that Bub1 S459 is followed by a proline, and matches the minimal Cdk1 substrate consensus of [S/T]P.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence analysis and known Cdk1 substrate specificity.

claim: Myc-Bub1 is phosphorylated at S459 in mitotic HeLa cells.
source: We next confirmed that Myc-Bub1 was indeed phosphorylated in mitotic HeLa cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cellular experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Bub1 S459 phosphorylation in mitosis is reduced upon treatment with the Mps1 inhibitor reversine.
source: Interestingly, Bub1 S459 phosphorylation in mitosis was reduced upon treatment of the Mps1 inhibitor, reversine.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cellular experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The effect of Mps1 inhibition on S459 phosphorylation may be indirect through checkpoint inactivation.
source: Because recombinant Bub1 protein was not phosphorylated at S459 by Mps1 in vitro, the effect of Mps1 inhibition on S459 phosphorylation may be indirectly through checkpoint inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between in vitro and cellular results.

claim: Bub1 S459 phosphorylation is regulated by the spindle checkpoint, possibly through the actions of phosphatases.
source: This result further suggests that Bub1 S459 phosphorylation is regulated by the spindle checkpoint, possibly through the actions of phosphatases.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that Mps1 inhibition reduces S459 phosphorylation.

claim: HeLa cells depleted of endogenous Bub1 have reduced mitotic index in the presence of taxol.
source: HeLa cells depleted of endogenous Bub1 with a small interfering RNA (siRNA) had reduced mitotic index in the presence of taxol, indicative of checkpoint defects (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The mitotic arrest deficiency caused by Bub1 depletion is rescued by ectopic expression of siRNA-resistant Bub1 full-length, but not the S459A mutant.
source: This mitotic arrest deficiency was rescued by ectopic expression of siRNA-resistant Bub1 full-length (FL), but not the S459A mutant (Figure 1D and E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a requirement for Bub1 S459 phosphorylation in the spindle checkpoint.
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Bub1 S459 phosphorylation is required for the spindle checkpoint.
source: This mitotic arrest deficiency was rescued by ectopic expression of siRNA-resistant Bub1 full-length (FL), but not the S459A mutant (Figure 1D and E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a requirement for Bub1 S459 phosphorylation in the spindle checkpoint.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments.

claim: Bub1 phosphorylates histone H2A and Cdc20 in mitosis.
source: In mitosis, Bub1 phosphorylates histone H2A and Cdc20 (Kawashima et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: H2A phosphorylation by Bub1 contributes to Shugoshin recruitment to kinetochores and protection of centromeric cohesion.
source: While H2A phosphorylation by Bub1 contributes to Shugoshin recruitment to kinetochores and protection of centromeric cohesion (Kawashima et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013a, 2015, 2013b), Bub1-mediated phosphorylation of Cdc20 contributes to the spindle checkpoint (Jia et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2008; Tang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Bub1-mediated phosphorylation of Cdc20 contributes to the spindle checkpoint.
source: While H2A phosphorylation by Bub1 contributes to Shugoshin recruitment to kinetochores and protection of centromeric cohesion (Kawashima et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013a, 2015, 2013b), Bub1-mediated phosphorylation of Cdc20 contributes to the spindle checkpoint (Jia et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2008; Tang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Bub1 FL and S459A exhibit comparable kinase activities towards Cdc20 S153 in vitro.
source: Bub1 FL and S459A exhibited comparable kinase activities towards Cdc20 S153 in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Bub1 S459 phosphorylation might contribute to checkpoint activation without compromising its kinase activity.
source: Therefore, Bub1 S459 phosphorylation might contribute to checkpoint activation without compromising its kinase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that S459A does not affect kinase activity but does affect checkpoint function.

claim: Bub1 has a scaffolding role in the spindle checkpoint.
source: Bub1 is known to have a scaffolding role in the spindle checkpoint (Jia et al., 2016; Klebig et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Expression of Bub1ΔK at higher levels restores the taxol-induced mitotic arrest of Bub1-depleted cells.
source: Indeed, expression of the Bub1 mutant lacking the kinase domain (Bub1ΔK) at higher levels restored the taxol-induced mitotic arrest of Bub1-depleted cells (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Bub1ΔK S459A fails to rescue the mitotic arrest deficiency caused by Bub1 depletion.
source: Bub1ΔK S459A failed to rescue the mitotic arrest deficiency caused by Bub1 depletion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The scaffolding function of the non-kinase region of Bub1 requires S459 phosphorylation.
source: This result suggests that the scaffolding function of the non-kinase region of Bub1 requires S459 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments with Bub1ΔK.

claim: Cells expressing Bub1FL stay in mitosis for about 6.7 hr in the presence of taxol before undergoing mitotic cell death or slippage.
source: In the presence of taxol, cells expressing Bub1FL or Bub1ΔK stayed in mitosis for about 6.7 hr or 4.7 hr, respectively, before undergoing mitotic cell death or slippage.
evidence: This is a primary finding from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cells expressing Bub1ΔK stay in mitosis for about 4.7 hr in the presence of taxol before undergoing mitotic cell death or slippage.
source: In the presence of taxol, cells expressing Bub1FL or Bub1ΔK stayed in mitosis for about 6.7 hr or 4.7 hr, respectively, before undergoing mitotic cell death or slippage.
evidence: This is a primary finding from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cells expressing Bub1ΔK S459A escape from mitosis after only about 3.2 hr in the presence of taxol.
source: Cells expressing Bub1ΔK S459A, however, escaped from mitosis after only about 3.2 hr (Figure 1F and Figure 1–figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In an unperturbed cell cycle, cells expressing Bub1ΔK S459A have a shorter mitotic duration (26 min) compared to cells expressing Bub1ΔK (47 min).
source: Furthermore, in an unperturbed cell cycle, cells expressing Bub1ΔK S459A had a shorter mitotic duration (26 min), as compared to cells expressing Bub1ΔK (47 min) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The non-kinase region of Bub1 has an important role in supporting the spindle checkpoint, and this role requires phosphorylation of S459 by Cdk1.
source: Collectively, these lines of evidence suggest the non-kinase region of Bub1 has an important role in supporting the spindle checkpoint, and this role requires phosphorylation of S459 by Cdk1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The middle region of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Bub1, when phosphorylated by Mps1, binds to Mad1–Mad2.
source: It has been reported previously that the middle region of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Bub1 (scBub1), when phosphorylated by Mps1, binds to Mad1–Mad2 and that this phosphorylation-dependent Bub1–Mad1 interaction is critical for the spindle checkpoint (London and Biggins, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The phosphorylation-dependent Bub1–Mad1 interaction is critical for the spindle checkpoint in yeast.
source: It has been reported previously that the middle region of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Bub1 (scBub1), when phosphorylated by Mps1, binds to Mad1–Mad2 and that this phosphorylation-dependent Bub1–Mad1 interaction is critical for the spindle checkpoint (London and Biggins, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Co-expression of scBub1369–608 with the kinase domain of scMps1 in bacteria leads to phosphorylation of the scBub1 fragment.
source: Co-expression of scBub1369–608 with the kinase domain of scMps1 in bacteria led to phosphorylation of the scBub1 fragment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from bacterial expression and pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only the phosphorylated scBub1 binds to the scMad1E–scMad2 complex.
source: Consistent with a previous report (London and Biggins, 2014), only the phosphorylated scBub1 bound to the scMad1E–scMad2 complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, consistent with previous work.

claim: Internal deletion of the CM renders scBub1369–608 unable to bind to scMad1–Mad2.
source: Internal deletion of the CM rendered scBub1369–608 unable to bind to scMad1–Mad2, indicating a requirement of this motif in this interaction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The CM motif is required for the scBub1–scMad1 interaction.
source: Internal deletion of the CM rendered scBub1369–608 unable to bind to scMad1–Mad2, indicating a requirement of this motif in this interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the deletion experiment.

claim: The phosphorylated scBub1449–530 fragment binds to scMad1–Mad2 with an affinity of 2.2 µM.
source: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) analysis showed that the smaller phosphorylated scBub1449–530 fragment containing the CM bound to scMad1–Mad2 with a moderate affinity of 2.2 µM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from ITC experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Phospho-scBub1 fragment binds to the CTD of scMad1 with a similar affinity as to scMad1–Mad2.
source: Interestingly, this phospho-scBub1 fragment bound to the CTD of scMad1 with a similar affinity, indicating that Mad1 CTD is sufficient for the scBub1–scMad1 interaction, and Mad2 and the MIM of Mad1 are not required for this interaction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from ITC experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mad1 CTD is sufficient for the scBub1–scMad1 interaction.
source: Interestingly, this phospho-scBub1 fragment bound to the CTD of scMad1 with a similar affinity, indicating that Mad1 CTD is sufficient for the scBub1–scMad1 interaction, and Mad2 and the MIM of Mad1 are not required for this interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ITC experiments.

claim: Mad2 and the MIM of Mad1 are not required for the scBub1–scMad1 interaction.
source: Interestingly, this phospho-scBub1 fragment bound to the CTD of scMad1 with a similar affinity, indicating that Mad1 CTD is sufficient for the scBub1–scMad1 interaction, and Mad2 and the MIM of Mad1 are not required for this interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ITC experiments.

claim: There are three conserved serine/threonine residues in the CM of scBub1: T453, T455 and S458.
source: There are three conserved serine/threonine residues in the CM of scBub1: T453, T455 and S458.
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequence analysis.

claim: All three residues (T453, T455, S458) are phosphorylated in scBub1449–530 co-expressed with scMps1.
source: Our mass spectrometry analysis revealed that all three residues were phosphorylated in scBub1449–530 co-expressed with scMps1.
evidence: This is a primary finding from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Both the singly phosphorylated pT455 peptide and the doubly phosphorylated pT453-pT455 peptide bind efficiently to scMad1 CTD.
source: Both the singly phosphorylated pT455 peptide and the doubly phosphorylated pT453-pT455 peptide, but not the singly phosphorylated pT453 peptide, bound efficiently to scMad1 CTD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The singly phosphorylated pT453 peptide does not bind efficiently to scMad1 CTD.
source: Both the singly phosphorylated pT455 peptide and the doubly phosphorylated pT453-pT455 peptide, but not the singly phosphorylated pT453 peptide, bound efficiently to scMad1 CTD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mutating the conserved RLK motif in Mad1 CTD abolishes scMad1 binding to both scBub1 phospho-CM peptides.
source: Mutating the conserved RLK motif in Mad1 CTD abolished scMad1 binding to both scBub1 phospho-CM peptides.
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The pT455 and pT453-pT455 peptides bind to scMad1 CTD with the same affinity.
source: Furthermore, ITC analysis showed that the pT455 and pT453-pT455 peptides bound to scMad1 CTD with the same affinity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from ITC experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mps1-dependent phosphorylation of scBub1 at T455 alone is sufficient to establish scBub1–scMad1 binding.
source: Thus, Mps1-dependent phosphorylation of scBub1 at T455 alone is sufficient to establish scBub1–scMad1 binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the peptide binding and ITC experiments.

claim: The scBub1–scMad1 interaction is mainly mediated by phospho-T455 of scBub1 and the RLK motif of scMad1.
source: The scBub1–scMad1 interaction is mainly mediated by phospho-T455 of scBub1 and the RLK motif of scMad1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the peptide binding and ITC experiments.

claim: Mutation of the T455 site in scBub1 disrupts scBub1–scMad1 binding and causes benomyl sensitivity in yeast cells.
source: We note that phosphorylation of the T455 site in scBub1 has been previously reported (London and Biggins, 2014), and mutation of this residue disrupts scBub1–scMad1 binding and causes benomyl sensitivity in yeast cells, establishing the functional relevance of this phosphorylation event.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The pT461 peptide of human Bub1 exhibits weak binding to human Mad1 CTD.
source: The pT461 peptide exhibited weak binding to human Mad1 CTD, and the doubly phosphorylated pS459-pT461 peptide had stronger binding (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The doubly phosphorylated pS459-pT461 peptide of human Bub1 has stronger binding to human Mad1 CTD than the pT461 peptide.
source: The pT461 peptide exhibited weak binding to human Mad1 CTD, and the doubly phosphorylated pS459-pT461 peptide had stronger binding (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Human Mad1 binds with higher affinity to the pS459-pT461 peptide than to the pT461 peptide.
source: ITC assays confirmed that human Mad1 bound with higher affinity to the pS459-pT461 peptide than to the pT461 peptide (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from ITC experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Binding of both pT461 and pS459-pT461 peptides to Mad1 is reduced by mutating the RLK motif in Mad1 CTD.
source: As a specificity control, binding of both peptides was reduced by mutating the RLK motif in Mad1 CTD.
evidence: This is a primary finding from ITC experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The triply phosphorylated pS459-pT461-pT464 peptide binds more weakly to Mad1 than the pS459-pT461 peptide.
source: Interestingly, the triply phosphorylated pS459-pT461-pT464 peptide bound more weakly to Mad1 than the pS459-pT461 peptide, indicating that phosphorylation of T464 had an inhibitory effect.
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Phosphorylation of T464 in human Bub1 has an inhibitory effect on Mad1 binding.
source: Interestingly, the triply phosphorylated pS459-pT461-pT464 peptide bound more weakly to Mad1 than the pS459-pT461 peptide, indicating that phosphorylation of T464 had an inhibitory effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the peptide binding experiments.

claim: Phosphorylation of both S459 and T461 of human Bub1 is required for its optimal interaction with Mad1.
source: Our results suggest that phosphorylation of both S459 and T461 of human Bub1 is required for its optimal interaction with Mad1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the peptide binding and ITC experiments.

claim: Incubation of recombinant Bub1ΔK–Bub3 with both Cdk1 and Mps1 leads to efficient phosphorylation of both S459 and T461.
source: Incubation of recombinant Bub1ΔK–Bub3 with both Cdk1 and Mps1 led to efficient phosphorylation of both residues, whereas incubation with either kinase did not (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Incubation of recombinant Bub1ΔK–Bub3 with either Cdk1 or Mps1 alone does not lead to efficient phosphorylation of both S459 and T461.
source: Incubation of recombinant Bub1ΔK–Bub3 with both Cdk1 and Mps1 led to efficient phosphorylation of both residues, whereas incubation with either kinase did not (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The pSpT antibody does not recognize the Bub1ΔKS459A/T461A (SATA) mutant treated with both Cdk1 and Mps1.
source: The pSpT antibody did not recognize the Bub1ΔKS459A/T461A (SATA) mutant treated with both Cdk1 and Mps1, demonstrating the specificity of the antibody.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cdk1 phosphorylation at S459 primes Mps1 phosphorylation at T461.
source: This result suggests that phosphorylation of Bub1 at S459 and T461 by Cdk1 and Mps1 occurs sequentially (Figure 2F). Cdk1 phosphorylation at S459 primes Mps1 phosphorylation at T461.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sequential kinase assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Phosphorylation of Bub1 at S459 and T461 by Cdk1 and Mps1 occurs sequentially.
source: This result suggests that phosphorylation of Bub1 at S459 and T461 by Cdk1 and Mps1 occurs sequentially (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sequential kinase assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mps1 prefers to phosphorylate sites with an acidic residue at the −2 position.
source: This notion is consistent with the fact that Mps1 prefers to phosphorylate sites with an acidic residue at the −2 position (Dou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: An interaction between human Bub1ΔK–Bub3 and GST-Mad1E–Mad2 is observed in vitro with both Cdk1- and Mps1-mediated phosphorylation.
source: With both Cdk1- and Mps1-mediated phosphorylation, we observed an interaction between human Bub1ΔK–Bub3 and GST-Mad1E–Mad2 in vitro (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Mutations of both phosphorylation sites on Bub1 or the RLK motif on Mad1 greatly reduce the Bub1–Mad1 interaction.
source: As important controls, mutations of both phosphorylation sites on Bub1 or the RLK motif on Mad1 greatly reduced this interaction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The phosphorylation-dependent interaction between Bub1 CM and Mad1 CTD is conserved from yeast to man.
source: Thus, the phosphorylation-dependent interaction between Bub1 CM and Mad1 CTD is conserved from yeast to man.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparative experiments in yeast and human systems.

claim: Bub1 T461 has been identified as a phospho-residue in a phospho-proteomics study.
source: Although we did not identify T461 as a phosphorylation site on endogenous human Bub1 isolated from mitotic HeLa cells, Bub1 T461 had been identified as a phospho-residue in a phospho-proteomics study (Daub et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Both S459 and T461 sites of Bub1 are phosphorylated in checkpoint-active cells.
source: Using the pSpT phospho-specific antibody, we confirmed that both S459 and T461 sites were phosphorylated in checkpoint-active cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cellular experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The T461A mutation greatly reduces the pS459 signal.
source: Interestingly, the T461A mutation also greatly reduced the pS459 signal.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cellular experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neither Bub1 T461A nor Bub1 SATA can rescue the mitotic arrest deficiency caused by depletion of endogenous Bub1.
source: Similar to Bub1 S459A, neither Bub1 T461A nor Bub1 SATA could rescue the mitotic arrest deficiency caused by depletion of endogenous Bub1 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Partial depletion of Bub1 and inhibition of Plk1 by BI 2536 synergistically inactivate the spindle checkpoint and reduce nocodazole-triggered mitotic arrest.
source: Moreover, as we showed previously (Jia et al., 2016), partial depletion of Bub1 and inhibition of Plk1 by BI 2536 synergistically inactivated the spindle checkpoint and reduced nocodazole-triggered mitotic arrest (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 3B, consistent with previous work.

claim: The mitotic arrest deficiency caused by partial Bub1 depletion and Plk1 inhibition is rescued by expression of siRNA-resistant Bub1 WT, but not S459A, T461A, or SATA.
source: This mitotic arrest deficiency was rescued by the expression of siRNA-resistant Bub1 WT, but not S459A, T461A, or SATA, indicating that phosphorylation of both sites on Bub1 are critical for checkpoint signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Phosphorylation of both S459 and T461 sites on Bub1 are critical for checkpoint signaling.
source: This mitotic arrest deficiency was rescued by the expression of siRNA-resistant Bub1 WT, but not S459A, T461A, or SATA, indicating that phosphorylation of both sites on Bub1 are critical for checkpoint signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments.

claim: Expression of the Mis12–Mad1 fusion protein causes spontaneous mitotic arrest.
source: Expression of the Mis12–Mad1 fusion protein caused spontaneous mitotic arrest, which was dependent on Mps1, BubR1, and Mad2, indicating that this arrest required an active spindle checkpoint (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The spontaneous mitotic arrest caused by Mis12–Mad1 fusion is dependent on Mps1, BubR1, and Mad2.
source: Expression of the Mis12–Mad1 fusion protein caused spontaneous mitotic arrest, which was dependent on Mps1, BubR1, and Mad2, indicating that this arrest required an active spindle checkpoint (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Mis12–Mad1 fusion proteins with the MIM or RLK motifs mutated fail to induce mitotic arrest.
source: Consistent with previous studies in yeast and human cells (Ballister et al., 2014; Heinrich et al., 2014), the Mis12–Mad1 fusion proteins with the MIM or RLK motifs mutated failed to induce the mitotic arrest.
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 3D, consistent with previous work.

claim: Both the Mad2-binding and Bub1-binding activities are critical for the checkpoint function of Mad1.
source: Thus, both the Mad2-binding and Bub1-binding activities are critical for the checkpoint function of Mad1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Mis12–Mad1 fusion experiments.

claim: The phosphorylation-dependent Bub1–Mad1 interaction is functionally important in the spindle checkpoint in human cells.
source: Taken together, our results establish the functional importance of the phosphorylation-dependent Bub1–Mad1 interaction in the spindle checkpoint in human cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Neither Bub1 nor Mad1 is a component of MCC.
source: Although neither Bub1 nor Mad1 is a component of MCC, they both directly interact with MCC components.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MCC composition.

claim: Bub1 and Mad1 both directly interact with MCC components.
source: Although neither Bub1 nor Mad1 is a component of MCC, they both directly interact with MCC components.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein interactions in the checkpoint.

claim: The constitutive Mad1–C-Mad2 complex interacts with O-Mad2 and converts it to I-Mad2.
source: The constitutive Mad1–C-Mad2 complex interacts with O-Mad2 and converts it to I-Mad2, which can bind to Cdc20 to form the Cdc20–C-Mad2 complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Mad2 activation.

claim: I-Mad2 can bind to Cdc20 to form the Cdc20–C-Mad2 complex.
source: The constitutive Mad1–C-Mad2 complex interacts with O-Mad2 and converts it to I-Mad2, which can bind to Cdc20 to form the Cdc20–C-Mad2 complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MCC assembly.

claim: Several previous studies have characterized the direct, checkpoint-relevant binding of Bub1 to Cdc20.
source: Furthermore, several previous studies have characterized the direct, checkpoint-relevant binding of Bub1 to Cdc20 (Di Fiore et al., 2015; Diaz-Martinez et al., 2015; Kang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The Bub1–Mad1 complex functions as a scaffold to recruit MCC components into close proximity, thus promoting MCC assembly.
source: These results raise the intriguing possibility that the Bub1–Mad1 complex functions as a scaffold to recruit MCC components (particularly I-Mad2 and Cdc20) into close proximity, thus promoting MCC assembly.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known interactions and the experimental findings.

claim: The N-terminal fragment of BubR1 (residues 1–370, BubR1N) supports the formation of functional MCC.
source: The N-terminal fragment of BubR1 (residues 1–370, BubR1N) has been shown previously to support the formation of functional MCC (Jia et al., 2016; Lara-Gonzalez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Monomeric Mad2 (Mad2Mono) is mostly the inactive O-Mad2.
source: The monomeric Mad2 (Mad2Mono) is mostly the inactive O-Mad2, while the dimeric Mad2 (Mad2Di) contains a mixture of dimers of active C-Mad2 and asymmetric dimers between C-Mad2 and I-Mad2 (Hara et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Dimeric Mad2 (Mad2Di) contains a mixture of dimers of active C-Mad2 and asymmetric dimers between C-Mad2 and I-Mad2.
source: The monomeric Mad2 (Mad2Mono) is mostly the inactive O-Mad2, while the dimeric Mad2 (Mad2Di) contains a mixture of dimers of active C-Mad2 and asymmetric dimers between C-Mad2 and I-Mad2 (Hara et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Incubation of BubR1N and Cdc20ΔN60 with Mad2Di allows the spontaneous formation of functional MCC that inhibits securin ubiquitination by APC/CCdc20.
source: Incubation of BubR1N and Cdc20ΔN60 with Mad2Di allowed the spontaneous formation of functional MCC that inhibited securin ubiquitination by APC/CCdc20.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mad2Mono is much less efficient in forming functional MCC than Mad2Di.
source: Mad2Mono was much less efficient in forming functional MCC and only showed weak APC/CCdc20 inhibition at very high doses.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The conformational change of Mad2 is a rate-limiting step in MCC assembly.
source: This result suggests that the conformational change of Mad2 is a rate-limiting step in MCC assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of Mad2Mono and Mad2Di in MCC assembly.

claim: Securin ubiquitination by APC/CCdc20 is strongly inhibited when the MCC mixture containing Mad2Mono is pre-incubated with the WT Bub1–Mad1 mixture.
source: Strikingly, securin ubiquitination by APC/CCdc20 was strongly inhibited when the MCC mixture containing Mad2Mono was pre-incubated with the WT Bub1–Mad1 mixture (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Omitting Mad2Mono abolishes APC/C inhibition in the reconstitution assay.
source: Omitting Mad2Mono abolished APC/C inhibition, indicating that MCC was formed by the activated Mad2Mono, and not by the C-Mad2 bound to Mad1.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MCC is formed by the activated Mad2Mono, and not by the C-Mad2 bound to Mad1.
source: Omitting Mad2Mono abolished APC/C inhibition, indicating that MCC was formed by the activated Mad2Mono, and not by the C-Mad2 bound to Mad1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reconstitution experiments.

claim: Mad1 overexpression abrogates the spindle checkpoint, presumably by titrating free Mad2.
source: This finding is consistent with the in vivo observation that Mad1 overexpression abrogates the spindle checkpoint, presumably by titrating free Mad2 (Chung and Chen, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Mps1 inhibition by reversine greatly weakens APC/CCdc20 inhibition by the MCC mixture.
source: Remarkably, Mps1 inhibition by reversine, mutations of S459 and T461 in Bub1 (SATA), or mutation of the Mad1 RLK motif (RLK/AAA) all greatly weakened APC/CCdc20 inhibition by the MCC mixture.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mutations of S459 and T461 in Bub1 (SATA) greatly weaken APC/CCdc20 inhibition by the MCC mixture.
source: Remarkably, Mps1 inhibition by reversine, mutations of S459 and T461 in Bub1 (SATA), or mutation of the Mad1 RLK motif (RLK/AAA) all greatly weakened APC/CCdc20 inhibition by the MCC mixture.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mutation of the Mad1 RLK motif (RLK/AAA) greatly weakens APC/CCdc20 inhibition by the MCC mixture.
source: Remarkably, Mps1 inhibition by reversine, mutations of S459 and T461 in Bub1 (SATA), or mutation of the Mad1 RLK motif (RLK/AAA) all greatly weakened APC/CCdc20 inhibition by the MCC mixture.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The intact phosphorylation-dependent Bub1–Mad1 interaction promotes APC/CCdc20 inhibition by the MCC mixture, presumably through facilitating Mad2 activation and MCC assembly.
source: These results indicate that the intact phosphorylation-dependent Bub1–Mad1 interaction promotes APC/CCdc20 inhibition by the MCC mixture, presumably through facilitating Mad2 activation and MCC assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reconstitution experiments, with the mechanism being inferred.

claim: In the presence of only Mad1E–Mad2 (without Bub1), Mps1 stimulates APC/CCdc20 inhibition by the MCC mixture containing Cdc20FL.
source: When testing different conditions for the in vitro reconstitution of Mps1-dependent APC/C inhibition by MCC, we noticed that, in the presence of only Mad1E–Mad2 (without Bub1), Mps1 stimulated APC/CCdc20 inhibition by the MCC mixture containing Cdc20FL (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Bub1-independent stimulatory effect of Mps1 is not observed with the MCC mixture containing Cdc20ΔN60.
source: Interestingly, this Bub1-independent stimulatory effect of Mps1 was not observed with the MCC mixture containing Cdc20ΔN60.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Overexpression of scMps1 in budding yeast causes constitutive activation of the spindle checkpoint and hyperphosphorylation of scMad1.
source: It has been reported previously that overexpression of scMps1 in the budding yeast causes constitutive activation of the spindle checkpoint and hyperphosphorylation of scMad1 (Hardwick et al., 1996), although the functional relevance of this Mps1-dependent Mad1 phosphorylation has not been further explored.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Incubation of the human Mad1E–Mad2 complex with human Mps1 and ATP slightly reduces the gel mobility of Mad1E.
source: Incubation of the human Mad1E–Mad2 complex with human Mps1 and ATP slightly reduced the gel mobility of Mad1E (Figure 5C), suggestive of Mad1 phosphorylation by Mps1.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 15 phosphorylation sites were identified in Mad1E by mass spectrometry, with 13 sites located in the flexible region N-terminal to the CTD.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis identified 15 phosphorylation sites in Mad1E, with 13 sites located in the flexible region N-terminal to the CTD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only two phosphorylation sites in Mad1E, T644 and T716, are located in Mad1 CTD.
source: Only two sites, T644 and T716, were located in Mad1 CTD, a domain known to be important for the spindle checkpoint (Figure 5D) (Heinrich et al., 2014; Kruse et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mad1 CTD is known to be important for the spindle checkpoint.
source: Only two sites, T644 and T716, were located in Mad1 CTD, a domain known to be important for the spindle checkpoint (Figure 5D) (Heinrich et al., 2014; Kruse et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Human Mps1 is a dual-specificity kinase.
source: Consistent with the initial discovery of human Mps1 as a dual-specificity kinase (Mills et al., 1992), a tyrosine residue in Mad1 was phosphorylated by Mps1.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A tyrosine residue in Mad1 is phosphorylated by Mps1.
source: Consistent with the initial discovery of human Mps1 as a dual-specificity kinase (Mills et al., 1992), a tyrosine residue in Mad1 was phosphorylated by Mps1.
evidence: This is a primary finding from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Mutating all identified phosphorylation sites in Mis12–Mad1 (YF-14A) abolishes the mitotic arrest exerted by this fusion protein.
source: Mutating all identified phosphorylation sites in Mis12–Mad1 (YF-14A) abolished the mitotic arrest exerted by this fusion protein.
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mutating the two sites in the CTD individually (T644A and T716A) abrogates the function of Mis12–Mad1 more strongly than simultaneously mutating the 13 sites outside of the CTD.
source: Strikingly, mutating the two sites in the CTD individually (T644A and T716A) abrogated the function of Mis12–Mad1 more strongly than simultaneously mutating the 13 sites outside of the CTD.
evidence: This is a primary finding from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ectopically expressed Mad1 (with its MIM mutated to alanine; MIM/5A) is phosphorylated at T716 during mitosis in human cells.
source: We thus generated a phospho-specific antibody against Mad1 phospho-T716, and confirmed that ectopically expressed Mad1 (with its MIM mutated to alanine prevent checkpoint inactivation; MIM/5A) was indeed phosphorylated at T716 during mitosis in human cells (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cellular experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Phosphorylation of Mad1 by Mps1 might be required for Mad1 function in human cells, with the two sites in the CTD being the most critical ones.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that phosphorylation of Mad1 by Mps1 might be required for Mad1 function in human cells, with the two sites in the CTD being the most critical ones.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Mis12–Mad1 fusion experiments.

claim: Mad1E–Mad2 WT, but not the phosphorylation-deficient YF-14A mutant, supports Mps1-dependent MCC formation and APC/C inhibition.
source: Mad1E–Mad2 WT, but not the phosphorylation-deficient YF-14A mutant, supported Mps1-dependent MCC formation and APC/C inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mutation of a single phosphorylation site T716 in Mad1 abolishes the stimulatory effect of Mps1 on MCC formation and APC/C inhibition.
source: Strikingly, mutation of a single phosphorylation site T716 in Mad1 abolished the stimulatory effect of Mps1.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Phosphorylation of Mad1 T716 by Mps1 enhances the formation of APC/C-inhibitory MCC in vitro.
source: Thus, phosphorylation of Mad1 T716 by Mps1 enhances the formation of APC/C-inhibitory MCC in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reconstitution experiments.

claim: The Mad1 T644A mutation does not affect the ability of Mps1 to stimulate MCC formation.
source: In contrast, the Mad1 T644A mutation did not affect the ability of Mps1 to stimulate MCC formation, suggesting that phosphorylation of this residue contributes to Mad1 function in vivo through other mechanisms.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Phosphorylation of Mad1 T644 contributes to Mad1 function in vivo through mechanisms other than MCC formation.
source: In contrast, the Mad1 T644A mutation did not affect the ability of Mps1 to stimulate MCC formation, suggesting that phosphorylation of this residue contributes to Mad1 function in vivo through other mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculation based on the discrepancy between in vitro and cellular results.

claim: Mutating the RLK motif of Mad1 abolishes the phospho-Mad1-dependent APC/C inhibition, even in the absence of Bub1.
source: Surprisingly, mutating the RLK motif of Mad1 also abolished the phospho-Mad1-dependent APC/C inhibition, even in the absence of Bub1 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The RLK motif has an additional function aside from binding to Bub1.
source: This result indicates that the RLK motif has an additional function aside from binding to Bub1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that RLK mutation affects APC/C inhibition even without Bub1.

claim: There are two copies of the RLK motif in each Mad1 CTD homodimer.
source: There are two copies of the RLK motif in each Mad1 CTD homodimer.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Mad1 structure.

claim: One RLK copy might bind to Bub1 while the other interacts with MCC components to facilitate MCC formation.
source: It is possible that one RLK copy binds to Bub1 while the other interacts with MCC components to facilitate MCC formation.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of the two RLK motifs.

claim: The RLK mutation might have unintended structural consequences.
source: Alternatively, the RLK mutation might have unintended structural consequences.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation for the RLK mutation effects.

claim: The N-terminal tail of Cdc20 contains two conserved basic motifs (BM1 and BM2).
source: As shown in Figure 5B, Mps1 and Mad1E–Mad2 only stimulated the APC/CCdc20-inhibitory activity of the MCC mixture containing Cdc20FL, but not that of the mixture containing Cdc20ΔN60. This suggests that Mps1-phosphorylated Mad1 might bind to the N-terminal tail of Cdc20, which contains two conserved basic motifs (BM1 and BM2) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mps1-phosphorylated Mad1 might bind to the N-terminal tail of Cdc20.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, Mps1 and Mad1E–Mad2 only stimulated the APC/CCdc20-inhibitory activity of the MCC mixture containing Cdc20FL, but not that of the mixture containing Cdc20ΔN60. This suggests that Mps1-phosphorylated Mad1 might bind to the N-terminal tail of Cdc20, which contains two conserved basic motifs (BM1 and BM2) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is speculation based on the differential effects with Cdc20FL and Cdc20ΔN60.

claim: The Mad1E–Mad2 complex pre-treated with the kinase domain of Mps1 is efficiently pulled down by the His6-tagged N-terminal fragment of Cdc20 (residues 1–170, Cdc20N).
source: Indeed, the Mad1E–Mad2 complex pre-treated with the kinase domain of Mps1 was efficiently pulled down by the His6-tagged N-terminal fragment of Cdc20 (residues 1–170, Cdc20N) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Inhibition of Mps1 by reversine greatly reduces the Mad1–Cdc20N interaction.
source: Inhibition of Mps1 by reversine greatly reduced this interaction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Mutating T716, but not all other phosphorylation sites, greatly diminishes the Mad1–Cdc20N interaction.
source: Mutating T716, but not all other phosphorylation sites, greatly diminished this interaction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Phosphorylation of Mad1 at T716 by Mps1 is necessary and sufficient for Cdc20N binding.
source: These results indicate that phosphorylation of Mad1 at T716 by Mps1 is necessary and sufficient for Cdc20N binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pull-down experiments.

claim: Residues 26–37 of Cdc20 are required for phospho-Mad1 binding.
source: Further mapping revealed a requirement for residues 26–37 of Cdc20 in phospho-Mad1 binding (Figure 6C and D), suggesting that BM1 (27RWQRK31) might be the binding site for Mad1 pT716.
evidence: This is a primary finding from pull-down experiments shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: BM1 (27RWQRK31) might be the binding site for Mad1 pT716.
source: Further mapping revealed a requirement for residues 26–37 of Cdc20 in phospho-Mad1 binding (Figure 6C and D), suggesting that BM1 (27RWQRK31) might be the binding site for Mad1 pT716.
evidence: This is speculation based on the mapping experiments.

claim: The phosphorylation-dependent binding between Mad1 CTD and Cdc20N might place the MIM of Cdc20 in the vicinity of I-Mad2, promoting the formation of Cdc20–C-Mad2 complex.
source: Because I-Mad2 binds to the Mad1-bound C-Mad2, this phosphorylation-dependent binding between Mad1 CTD and Cdc20N might place the MIM of Cdc20 in the vicinity of I-Mad2, promoting the formation of Cdc20–C-Mad2 complex, which can further bind BubR1 to form MCC.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism by which phospho-Mad1 promotes MCC assembly.

claim: Mps1 can phosphorylate Knl1 at multiple MELT motifs to recruit the Bub1–Bub3 complex to kinetochores.
source: It is well established that Mps1 can phosphorylate Knl1 at multiple MELT motifs to recruit the Bub1–Bub3 complex to kinetochores (Krenn et al., 2014; London et al., 2012; Primorac et al., 2013; Shepperd et al., 2012; Vleugel et al., 2013; Yamagishi et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mps1-dependent Bub1–Mad1 interaction has been characterized in the budding and fission yeast.
source: Mps1-dependent Bub1–Mad1 interaction has also been characterized in the budding and fission yeast (London and Biggins, 2014; Mora-Santos et al., 2016), but has so far not been reported in humans.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: After priming phosphorylation by Cdk1, human Mps1 can phosphorylate the conserved motif of human Bub1, which enables the binding of human Mad1.
source: In the current study, we have shown that after priming phosphorylation by Cdk1, human Mps1 can phosphorylate the conserved motif of human Bub1, which enables the binding of human Mad1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Bub1 is another evolutionarily conserved substrate of Mps1.
source: Therefore, Bub1 is another evolutionarily conserved substrate of Mps1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings in both yeast and human systems.

claim: Phospho-Bub1–Mad1-dependent APC/C inhibition by MCC components has been reconstituted in vitro.
source: We have reconstituted phospho-Bub1–Mad1-dependent APC/C inhibition by MCC components in vitro and demonstrated a requirement for this interaction in the spindle checkpoint in human cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The Bub1–Mad1 interaction is required for the spindle checkpoint in human cells.
source: We have reconstituted phospho-Bub1–Mad1-dependent APC/C inhibition by MCC components in vitro and demonstrated a requirement for this interaction in the spindle checkpoint in human cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Novel phosphorylation events of Mad1 by Mps1 are required for checkpoint activation and APC/C inhibition.
source: In addition, we have identified novel phosphorylation events of Mad1 by Mps1, which are also required for checkpoint activation and APC/C inhibition.
